title: Short Stuff: Goosebumps
summary: Short Stuff episode on goose bumps (piloerection). Josh and Chuck open with a tangent about R. L. Stein's Goosebumps books and the Netflix series Fear Street, then explain goose bumps as an evolutionary holdover: trapping warmth and making animals look bigger to predators. They note that goose bumps are rare among sympathetic nervous responses in being consciously controllable. They then discuss why music and emotional moments trigger chills, citing a January study in Biological Psychology that used Celine Dion's "My Heart Will Go On" and Prince's "Purple Rain," Mitchell Culver's dual-brain (emotional vs. rational) threat-and-relief hypothesis, and Jaak Panksepp's 2011 separation-call hypothesis. The hosts stress that these are hypotheses, not settled science.

segments.title: Opening banter and Goosebumps books
segments.summary: Hosts joke about R. L. Stein's Goosebumps books being below their age range and recommend Stein's Netflix series Fear Street as a gory, adult horror show.

segments.title: Goose bumps as an evolutionary holdover
segments.summary: Goose bumps (piloerection) are explained as the pilo erector muscles raising hair or skin, an evolutionary holdover. Functions discussed: trapping warm air for warmth and making animals look bigger to predators, tied to the fight-or-flight response of the sympathetic nervous system. Goose bumps are noted as unusual because some people can trigger them consciously.

segments.title: Why humans get chills from emotional moments
segments.summary: The hosts note that in humans the goose bump response has been hijacked by emotionally evocative things such as live concert moments, with a Boston drum solo used as an example.

segments.title: Chills study: Celine Dion and Prince
segments.summary: A study in Biological Psychology, published in January, measured subjective chills and piloerection ratios while listeners heard songs. My Heart Will Go On had a 14 percent piloerection ratio. Purple Rain produced chills in every participant and goose bumps in half, with the strongest response at Prince's vocal wail near the end, where a solo voice emerges from a complex arrangement.

segments.title: Competing theories: Culver's dual-brain hypothesis and the separation call
segments.summary: Mitchell Culver's hypothesis holds that an emotional brain perceives surprises as threats, and the rational brain then resolves them, releasing built-up attention as a pleasant feeling and possibly dopamine. The hosts say this is a hypothesis, not settled science, and question the dopamine explanation. Jaak Panksepp's 2011 study proposed that a solo voice or instrument mimics a separation call and triggers a sense of loss. The hosts say they favor the separation-call idea.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: The hosts wrap up the short and sign off, with a note that Stuff You Should Know is an iHeartRadio production.
